# Command-Line for Mac

The macOS command line interface, accessible via the Terminal application, uses a Unix-based shell (by default, this is Bash or Zsh in newer versions). Familiarity with the command line can significantly enhance your productivity by enabling you to perform tasks that would otherwise require more time-consuming graphical interfaces.

## Starting the Terminal

To open the Terminal in macOS, you can use Spotlight Search (`Cmd + Space`) and type "Terminal," or navigate through `Applications -> Utilities -> Terminal`.

## Useful Commands

Below is a summary of some essential commands that every user should know when working on macOS or any Unix-like operating system.

| Command (Mac OS / Linux) | Description                         | Example                                    |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `pwd`                    | Show the current directory          | `pwd`                                      |
| `ls`                     | List directories and files          | `ls`, `ls -l` for detailed list            |
| `cd`                     | Change directory                    | `cd test`, `cd ..`                         |
| `mkdir`                  | Create a new directory              | `mkdir newfolder`                          |
| `cp`                     | Copy files or directories           | `cp source.txt destination.txt`            |
| `mv`                     | Move or rename files or directories | `mv oldname.txt newname.txt`               |
| `rm`                     | Delete a file                       | `rm unwanted.txt`                          |
| `rm -r`                  | Delete a directory recursively      | `rm -r oldfolder`                          |
| `man [command]`          | Get help for a command              | `man ls`                                   |
| `exit`                   | Close the terminal window           | `exit`                                     |

## Additional Tips

- **Navigating Directories**: Use `cd ..` to go up one level, or `cd` to go directly to your home directory.
- **Listing Options**: `ls -a` lists all files, including hidden ones that start with a dot (`.`).
- **Wildcard Usage**: Use wildcards (`*`) with commands like `ls`, `cp`, or `rm` to affect multiple files. For example, `rm *.txt` would remove all text files in the current directory.
- **Viewing Files**: Use `cat [file]` to display the content of a file, or `less [file]` to view it in an interactable mode.

:::{.callout-note}
Many commands can be modified with various options, also known as "flags," which can be combined to achieve different effects. For instance, `ls -lt` lists files in long format sorted by modification time. Experimenting with these can help you find the most efficient ways to work.
:::

Understanding these commands can help you navigate and manage your files effectively, automate tasks using scripts, and use advanced features of the macOS environment. This knowledge is essential for anyone looking to enhance their proficiency with macOS or Linux systems.
